utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Dr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, good morning to you. Please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Parsons. I beg your pardon. Yesterday we started dealing with this topic. Do you have a single database or does it have some subdivisions or strata?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer that I gave yesterday to that question was that we do maintain a single database within a forensic data management system, but it is divided into subprojects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us which subprojects exist in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina, or is Bosnia-Herzegovina a single subproject?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina is a single subproject.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, when you work on the identification of DNA profiles from all the Bosnian theatres of war, you have a single database and a single code, a single code number, a general code number; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These numbers that are ahead of the bar codes in your identifications, for example, when it starts with an 8 or a 9, for instance, 910, or 810, et cetera, does that mean anything? Is that something that should be recognised? Is that something that has a meaning of its own?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The initial number associated with the bar code indicates some type of a subdivision within the database. So ones beginning with 9 would represent mortal remains samples, human remains samples, from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do any of the subsequent numbers further determine or further specify the position, the origin, of that sample?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Everything after that is completely randomised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the bar code, is there a number that denotes the type of material involved?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the bar code, no. It has absolutely no information about the sample whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In 4107, that's the 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, could we please call up this document. 4107. Actually, 4170. 246. Could we have that, please. 246 would be the ERN number. Page 5 in e-court, or, actually, in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this to us now: What are these numbers that denote bar codes for blood; and are they different from the bone bar codes?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It appears to me that you are referring to the first number of lines on this page and where we have listed blood, bone, mini, and then it shows the initial numbers from the bar codes that are associated with those different categories, consistent with what I had explained a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do the bar codes start for other locations outside Bosnia, outside the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have different numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, for example, within Bosnia-Herzegovina, do all the numbers from Srebrenica start with the number 9 or -- or how do you know it is Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire point of our blinding system involving ascribing bar codes to samples is that the DNA laboratory, when they work on these remains, are unaware where they come from. So, indeed, it is the case that all Srebrenica remains have the beginning 9 in the bar code number but so do all the other mortal remains from Bosnia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But then when you establish probability, which number do you take as the number of missing persons? 1 to what?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we have gone through the process to the point where a match has actually been made, then the DNA process has been finished at that point. It is at that point where the identification co-ordination division establishes a DNA match report. And in that instance they take account of two things, at least. One, being where the individual was reported missing from that has been matched. And then, secondly, and very importantly, where the sample did originate from; what grave, for example. In the case of Srebrenica it would one of the graves known to the ICTY and ICMP as being Srebrenica related.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, again, the material is given a name and surname. And there is no more anonymity; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the point of the identification process, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who hands over this material. Yesterday we said that it was the pathologist. How can we be sure that the material that arrived in the lab had not been taken elsewhere from a location or, rather, from some bodies, mortal remains, that do not belong to the target group that you are studying?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that depends on a number of factors. In many instances the ICMP archeological teams have been present at the recovery and very carefully remove the remains from the grave with extremely high standards of evidentiary documentation, and in many instances of those, they were transferred to the Podrinje identification project mortuary where the ICMP maintains seconded expert staff. And in those instances, many, many of those instances, we would consider that the samples have been under the custody or at least observation of the ICMP continuously. However, it is the case that we do receive samples from any number of contributors, pathologists, as I mentioned before, et cetera, where we're not directly involved in the -- in the recovery or all sets -- all steps of handling of the remains, and then, therefore, the chain of command that we maintain originates when that sample comes to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now give us the alternative sources of samples. What are the other places from which the sample could have arrived?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there have been a number of mortuary facilities throughout the former Yugoslavia, Bosnia, where we received samples. Most of them from Srebrenica do go through the Podrinje identification project, others in a commemorative centre in Tuzla, and for some time there was a mortuary facility in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say that this centre was Podrinje was in Kalesija? The autopsy centre, in the autopsy room.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know where Kalesija is. The Podrinje identification project centre is in Tuzla, in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. So in Tuzla itself, we have two types of samples: Those that are under your control; and those that come from the mortuary in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which mortuary are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, a moment ago, you said that there were alternative sources of material, of samples, and that they originated from an autopsy room, or whatever you said, in Tuzla, Visoko, and from this identification centre in Podrinje. What are all the places from which you could have and, indeed, did receive samples?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To attempt to clarify a little bit, you've mentioned several times a centre called Kalesija. I don't know what you are referring to there. There's a clinical centre in Tuzla which is not related to the ICMP. There's the Podrinje identification project, also in Tuzla, you are correct, that is highly related to the ICMP. And then there are any number of other mortuary facilities through which a very small number of samples related to Srebrenica would have passed, including, for a short period of time, one in the town of Visoko. I'm not able to give you a complete list by memory of these places where they would originate, but, again, I would emphasise a very, very small number that were not -- that did not pass through the Podrinje identification project.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's what it's all about. In Tuzla, we have two sources of material, of samples. One is under your control; one is in the clinical centre; and there is a third one in Visoko. Those are the major ones involved. Are you trying to say that you do not know that in Kalesija there was an autopsy centre, and during autopsies, material was being taken for DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this would be the third time that I stated that I am unfamiliar with the name Kalesija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. On the basis of your notes, can we get information about these other mortuaries that could have sent material and that, indeed, did send material?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ICMP would have the information as to where those came from, yeah, in the some 15.000 samples that have been processed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 15.000 samples in relation to all of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There are almost 15.000 DNA match reports relating to individual samples specifically related to Srebrenica. So I misspoke. The total number would be higher than those that have been DNA matched.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in relation to Srebrenica, in July 1995, you found 15.000 pairs, am I right, or, rather, matches? One side of the pair or match is the victim; and the other side is the relative.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a broad general statement, I would answer in the affirmative. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we have 15.000 victims in Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That question betrays a lack of understanding of the nature of our DNA match reports, and the context of the identification. I said that there were almost 15.000 DNA match reports, each one of which relates to a separate sample submitted for identification. The problem that is faced in Srebrenica is that the large primary graves that were established at a particular point in time in July 1995 were subsequently disrupted by heavy machinery and transferred to a large series of clandestine secondary mass graves throughout the country-side. This resulted in fragmentation and destruction of the mortal remains in a manner that caused multiple DNA tests to be applied to different body parts, and these body parts from the same individual may be in multiple different graves. And in fact, we have DNA linkages between the primary graves, between some of the execution sites, and then a large number of secondary mass graves that shows the patterns of linkage between these sites. So the 15.000 that we're referring to are different samples that have been related to specific identified victims. I stated yesterday that we have DNA evidence reflecting 6.772 unique victims associated with the Srebrenica event. Many of the 15.000 DNA match reports are multiple samples from the same individuals that have been recovered from fragmentary remains in secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So then we have to assume that about two and a half samples belong to a single individual, on average. What is the largest number of samples that pertained to a single individual, or a single body? If it's 6.000-something, I mean, if we divide 15.000 by 6.000-something, we get 2.5, 2.8, on average. Samples from a single body, that is. So what would the largest number be of samples that were taken in relation to a single body; and what was the smallest number? So what were the statistics in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your last question is what were the statistics, and I cannot give you a, by memory, distribution, nor can I tell you that I know for sure what the maximum number is, but I think can I give you useful information that we do have some cases -- the largest that I have in mind is 15 different DNA matches that were required to assemble the entire body. And it's not rare that there are multiple ones, four, five, eight sometimes. However, you also asked about the minimum number, and that obviously would be one, and there are quite a few of those as well. I'll mention also that it is by no means the case that all these people who had been DNA matched had been fully reassociated. In many instances, we're still missing portions of these bodies. If we were able to recover all the remains and put them together, it would require yet additional DNA matches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go a bit to -- back to the previous probability. Do you know what the total number of missing persons is that should be taken into account for setting the posterior probability, is it 29.000-something?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we perform calculations on samples considered by their location and then, eventually, by the individual that is being matched by virtue of the -- place of reported missing, we use nominally today a value of 1 in 7.000. That's based on the fact that -- there's a little bit of a -- actually there's a little bit of a historical component to this. And the fact of the matter is that the details of this number are not extremely important with regard to our DNA match threshold. So we consider based on the fact that we have about 7800 missing individuals reported to us from Srebrenica and our matching rate, that there are some 8.000 to 8.100 individuals associated with the Srebrenica event. At the time we started performing statistical calculations, already quite a few had been identified so we chose the remaining number of unidentified at that time to be about 1 in 7.000. And so that's the prior probability that we have used then. In point of fact, once you have identified someone, it's no longer possible that a different DNA profile comes from that individual, so we could have, and maybe should have, lowered the prior probability sequentially as we made identifications. So today now that we have identified 6.772, probably the better prior probability would be 8.000 minus 6.772 remaining unidentified victims. But, in fact, we simply haven't taken the step of changing that calculation. Using the larger number is conservative, meaning it -- it's a higher bar for identification, but small changes by factors of two or three in the prior probability simply don't affect the vast statistics that are obtained from DNA. So we don't take the step of routinely altering the prior probability.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Wouldn't it be even more conservative and more accurate if you took, say, 1 to 29.000, which is the number of people that are being looked for in Bosnia that were included in your single database?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be more conservative. It would also be more conservative to use the number of people that have ever existed on Earth. But you also posed the question with regard to accuracy. And, no, it would not be more accurate to use the 1 in 29.000. Because of the regional distribution and what we know about where the remains come from, the most accurate number would be those associated with the Srebrenica event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you trying to say that you excluded population movements during the war, and that in the area of Podrinje, no one from Tuzla, Doboj, or any other part of Bosnia-Herzegovina was killed?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're not saying what you just suggested, but it doesn't follow from my previous answer concerning prior probabilities either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it does concern the issue of 7.000. Why 7.000, when the samples could contain the remains of people from all over Bosnia-Herzegovina, because it was all within a single theatre of war where units moved or went through?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's simply not the case that -- that -- that it's a reasonable probability that someone killed in Operation Flash and Storm in Western Bosnia was recovered from a Srebrenica-related grave near Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll leave Flash and Storm aside as it is in Croatia. But do you know that units of the Army of the Bosnia-Herzegovina were mobile, and that both individuals and parts of units, and groups moved from one part of the front to another? And not only Muslim units, but Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to state any knowledge about movements of Bosnian army troops. I'm simply reporting what is known with -- by virtue of reported missing individuals from particular regions and particular events in Bosnia. That's quite a bit different, I think, than the assertion that armies moved around, which I, no doubt, believe is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In that case, would prior probability be different if you took 1 to 30.000? Would the result of 99.9999 be different?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Changing the prior probability will change the final statistic. If you remember, our minimum threshold for identification for issuing a DNA match report, was 99.95 per cent. Now, on our DNA match reports, the maximum number of 9s that we use after the decimal point is five. And that's because we don't bother to continue to list the 9s. So changing the prior probability from 1 in 7.000 to 1 in 30.000 would maybe remove one of those 9s from a list of 11 or 12 9s after the decimal point. So in a vast majority - virtually all - of the DNA match reports we've issued, we would still be way in excess of the minimum required surety for issuing a match report, regardless of whether the value was in 1 in 7.000, 1 in 2.500, which is probably the more accurate value now, or 1 in 30.000. It is simply an identification process that is extremely robust to variations in the prior probability of the order of magnitude that we are discussing here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If this is so, then why didn't you take 30.000, but you took 7.000, if there was no danger of your results being influenced significantly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the doctor has answered the question. Why don't you move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After identification, did you notice that there was a significant amount of people who were not from Srebrenica? In other words, they were born elsewhere or belonged to a different unit. Did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've taken no account of where people are born. This was a United Nations safe haven that harboured refugees from all over the area. The operational information that we're involved with is where the individual has been reported missing from. And, in fact, no, we have not noted a large number of individuals recovered from these graves who are reported from places elsewhere than Srebrenica. In fact, virtually none.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you currently reside in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you kept up to date with the new findings of the Bosnian side about the number of missing, the number of people from Srebrenica, and generally with any new developments regarding Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can answer your question usefully, but it would probably be wise for both parties for you to clarify what you mean by "from the Bosnian side."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Muslim side. You are correct: We are all Bosnian. But the Muslims grabbed the term to designate themselves.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to know precisely how to address such a question but -- because I think it is sort of fundamentally unanswerable as posed. Let me just make a few comments that may relate to what -- to some elements that you have in mind. Yes, I am extremely well apprised of the continuing developments of the ICMP identification project with regard to Srebrenica, as well as all the other areas that the ICMP works in. I am continually and on an ongoing basis working with my colleagues in Sarajevo, in Tuzla, and in the archaeology and anthropology teams. The ICMP doesn't operate in a realm that considers a Muslim side or any other side. We try to identify people missing from the conflict in the former Yugoslavia without reference to religion, ethnicity or any other factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Serb side is completely dissatisfied and that the disproportionate amounts of identified individuals is much to the detriment of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you define "the Serb side," please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you must have been told, there was an interethnic conflict between the Bosnian Serbs, Bosnian Muslims, and Bosnian Croats. The Bosnian Serbs had proportionally the same amount of losses as the other two peoples. The Croats did have somewhat less than the Muslims, but the Serb sides [as interpreted] were proportionate. Now, the Serb side is basically completely dissatisfied with the identification of its own people who had gone missing. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just still don't know how mean by "the Serb side." You're asking me to comment on the state of mind of individuals that you haven't identified in any useful manner to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, it is not about the state of mind of an individual but about institutions. Republika Srpska, the association of families of those killed and missing, they are all now leaving the joint institutions as they have concluded that the institutions in question are not busy with trying to identify the missing Serbs. Are you trying to say that are you completely unaware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not completely unaware of some dissatisfaction that has been expressed by either agencies related to the Republika Srpska or, in fact, some family organisations, and then some incendiary press as well. I can only say that the ICMP's work is entirely unbiased and we are delighted to identify anyone that we are able to do so in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the proportion between the identified mortal remains or individuals of Muslim, as opposed to Serb ethnicity? Perhaps we should look into whether this dissatisfaction is justified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What -- I -- the doctor has answered the question about the dissatisfaction. I don't follow your question. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, the question was unclear, and also I don't think it is relative or germane to the issues that Dr. Parsons has been discussing. So I would object to it on that basis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am simply testing the origin, the financing, and reliability of that institution, as well as their accuracy and potential bias. This is what this Defence is trying to test here. The Serb side in Bosnia-Herzegovina has strong objections. I have -- I mean to say Serb officials, not individuals. Still, the results show that they may well be right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is this: What is the ratio of those identified on the Serb side as opposed to those on the Muslim side? Perhaps we should look into whether the dissatisfaction in question is based on sound facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just ask one question. Your last comment is just an unnecessary statement on your part. How many Serbs and how many Muslims have been identified may be a fair question for the doctor to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the answer is that the ICMP does not track the ethnicity of individuals that it identifies. Again this is related to our fundamental charter of -- of unbiased action. We don't ask somebody, Is your missing person a Serb, is your missing person a Muslim, and we don't track those statistics in any way. Those would be, in fact, a basis by which we could exercise bias or be perceived to exercise bias. We simply don't operate that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will put my position and the position of this Defence. You are either biased or intentionally confused by your hosts who served your task upon you, so to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that is not a question. That's a statement and an assertion of fact with no evidential basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But that is Dr. Karadzic's case and you may comment upon that, Dr. Parsons. If you so wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We're certainly not biased and I don't know who you mean by "hosts." We provide DNA assistance to the government of Bosnia under the auspices of the Missing Persons Institute which was established as a national body responsible for identification of missing persons without regard to ethnicity. But I wouldn't call them our hosts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you part of that institute? As you said that you worked under "their auspices." Are you not a director of that institute?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not a director of that institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is your position then? What are you, in the organisational sense, institutional sense?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm the director of forensic science of the International Commission on Missing Persons, which is not a part of the Missing Persons Institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll leave that topic then. Did you hear that the Bosnian side, the Muslim side, on several occasions stated that there are irregularities surrounding Srebrenica. Some ten months ago, they stated that there were 500 living people and 70 people who had been killed elsewhere. Have you heard of this initial statement and the figures?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "the Muslim side." And, so, therefore, no, I am unaware of anything that you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This institution you call the national institute, it is an institution in Sarajevo controlled by the Muslim side. If you are so naive and so not acquainted with the area you worked in, and if you don't know that there were three ethnicities at war there, then I, indeed, understand why you have no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I obviously object to the question. It is argumentative and I think it's unnecessary in light of the tenor of the -- Dr. Parsons's testimony and the examination so far. If he has a direct question to put to Dr. Parsons, I don't see why he doesn't just do that. But I think the hyperbole is unnecessary in this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we agree, of course. Mr. Karadzic, just put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, are you trying to avoid providing answers by resorting to statements such as you being unaware of what "the Muslim side" means, or is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just clarify what you meant by "Muslim side." That's sufficient, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, do you know that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, three ethnic communities were at war and that Bosnia came out as a reorganised state with three constituent peoples and two entities?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the institutions in Sarajevo - not in East Sarajevo but in the Federal Sarajevo - are completely controlled by one of the three ethnic groups, which is the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You made a reference to "the institutions in Sarajevo." I have no idea what institutions you refer to. If you ask me a specific question, I will give you a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say the Institute for Missing Persons that your ICMP co-operates with. Have you heard of Amor Masovic, Mirsad Tokaca and other prominent representatives of the Muslim side involving the task of search and identification?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned three things specific there that are different from one another. One is the Missing Persons Institute which is not Muslim controlled. It is, in fact, a national organisation that is constituted with a directorate from each of the three previous ethnic groups. One of whom is Amor Masovic. Mirsad Tokaca is an individual I don't know much about and but, as far as I'm aware, is not associated with the Missing Persons Institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that these structures - that you claim to be national rather than ethnic - on a number of occasions stated that the situation around Srebrenica was unclear? At first, they said there were 500 people who were still alive and 70 people who did not die in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would ask that if Dr. Karadzic has a specific reference to those statements that he -- that he put that to the witness or provide it for the benefit of the witness and the Chamber in e-court. If he has it. Otherwise, I'm sure that I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before putting the document, is he not entitled to ask a question for the doctor? Whether this institution or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether the doctor knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. The nature of the objection, Mr. President, is that there's no evidence in the record yet as to what these institutes have represented. So if the question is does he know that they have made that representation, then he is assuming a fact which is not yet in evidence in this case, as far as I'm aware. Certainly not in the context of this witness's testimony. If he has heard -- if the question is has he heard something of that nature, rather than the specific attribution to the institute or the centre, then that's a different question. But as he has phrased it, it's assuming a fact that's not in evidence in this case and that is the basis of the objection. And that's the reason why I have asked him to put that evidence into the case in order to pose the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Karadzic, could you be more specific as to these structures or by -- or what you meant by "they" in putting that question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will seek to tender the appropriate documents when the time is right. But I'm simply interested now in the basis of information of Dr. Parsons. I'm interested in his knowledge. Mirsad Tokaca and Amor Masovic on two occasions publicly stated the first time around that there were 500 people who are still alive who were included on the list of victims by mistake and that there are another 70 people who were killed in another place at a different time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would like the Court to understand that I'm not wholly ignorant of the context in which -- that he is referring to. But, again, he -- he -- Mr. Karadzic makes statements that are very difficult for me to respond to specifically. First of all, I don't follow this information very closely at all. I concern myself with the forensic activities of the ICMP with regard to definitive analyses of forensic expertise. With regard -- the biggest variable I have here -- I do know that Mirsad Tokaca in his research -- his private research undertakings has made reference to some individuals that, in some manner or other, have been listed as victims of Srebrenica that -- that he claims - and I am familiar with the number 500, very roughly - aren't actually the victims. But I would like to postulate or, let me say, state, that these lists of missing persons are very dynamic things to try to resolve. So at the outset -- at the conclusion of a conflict there are going to be many, many people reported missing and it takes a long time for these lists -- and different people maintain lists, the ICRC maintains a list. This research undertaken by Tokaca has set out to do that. I don't know what list these 500 were supposedly on that he now claims that they shouldn't be on. I can tell you that I think it's -- that I don't believe it's on the list of individuals that the ICMP has identified by DNA. I do not believe that that's the case. And if he were to say so, I would say he's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that recently something was stated that had to concern you as well. That some persons were still alive but that their amputated body parts reached the DNA lab. Now this is what I'm interested in. How was that possible? How was it possible for the material of living persons to appear in the DNA lab? Amputees from operating rooms, their body parts were found in mass graves. How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of those allegations. I consider them to be extremely unlikely to be true. But, not having any information, I can't comment further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Parsons, with all due respect, these are not accusations. These are admissions. The Muslim side admitted that there were several hundred persons whose amputated body parts reached the DNA lab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the doctor has said that he doesn't know of such allegation. Then you say Muslim side admitted such and such. Be specific or avoid a repetition.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, my correction had to do with what was stated, that these were accusations. No, the Muslim side admitted publicly that some body parts of amputees reached the DNA lab, and that directly has to do with Dr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what, Mr. Karadzic. The doctor said he doesn't know. You put to him specific information you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would like to make one -- one comment is, first of all, you are correct, Your Honour. I am unaware of these allegations. But these people that were amputees would not be reported missing to us by the families from Srebrenica, and I consider it completely improbable that any of them -- any of these putative samples that come from amputees would be on this list of DNA matches to Srebrenica victims that has been presented to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to move on from this topic, and we're going to show that when the time comes. This is what I'd like to ask you now: What did the base of kinsmen look like? What does that exactly imply?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have a family reference genetic database of -- obtained from blood samples of family members that are seeking the persons missing from the conflict. I don't know much more about what I can say about that. Can you please clarify what it is about that database you would like me to comment on, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The line of kinship that you took into consideration.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, you want to obtain reference samples from the most closely related individuals as possible. So ideal donors for a missing individual would be his parents. Those are what are considered to be first-degree relatives. The missing person's children are also first-degree relatives, and particularly if you can also obtain a DNA profile from the spouse, children are very, very helpful for an identification process. Siblings are very useful particularly in combination with, for example, one parent, and that's a common situation that we might have in Srebrenica where we would have a mother and maybe a sister or two that are able to provide a reference sample. More distant relatives, aunts and uncles and cousins, by themselves are generally not particularly useful but sometimes in combination with other sets of relatives are useful. And so we do collect as many reference samples as we can get at the outset because we don't know the details of who we're going to, in the end, completely collect for a particular individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the average number of relatives that you dealt with for a single missing person? And what is the maximum number?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't tell you the maximum number. I really don't know. But our average number, the ratio of reference samples to reported missing persons, is just slightly over three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a separate database of DNA of relatives of the missing from Srebrenica separate from missing persons in other areas in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's not. Any bone sample coming to us from anywhere in Bosnia is compared to all the reference profiles that we have from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a separate database for the relatives of members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a database for relatives of missing persons who are not related to the second week of July 1995 in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give you the same answer I gave you a moment ago: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have a database of relatives of Serbs and others who lived in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica and who are missing?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. DNA profiles from bone samples from the mass grave that the Prosecution links up with Srebrenica in July 1995, were they compared to other databases of relatives of other missing persons?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That's the answer I gave a moment ago as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In which way did the ICMP obtain the names of missing persons?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through a massive public outreach effort that took place all over the former Yugoslavia and even extended internationally to try to cover the diaspora of refugees and people that emigrated from the war. So we had a public information campaign, set up many centres around Bosnia and continue to this day to maintain standing facilities where family members can come forward and report a missing person, report the circumstances of that person's disappearance, in general, and then, most importantly, provide a reference sample that would allow us to match that missing person to the family should remains from that missing person ever be submitted to our DNA laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did the ICMP check this; and, if so, how did they do this? Did the persons who were reported as missing really go missing in relation to what had happened in the second week of July in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ICMP has not conducted investigations into individual cases in that manner, no. We record the information that the family members report to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you said that you worked on the basis of an assumption that you had developed, that the ICMP had developed; namely, that this has to do with persons that are linked to what happened in Srebrenica in July 1995. What is your position now? Are you saying that what you identified were victims from the second week of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me talk a little bit about how names come to be listed on the DNA match report list that we described yesterday. In the first instance, and a most important initial element for someone to be listed on that list, is that the family member reported the individual missing from the fall of Srebrenica in 1995 with the designations of either missing with regard to having departed overland, to try to reach Tuzla in the days prior to July 10 and 11, or in having remained in the so-called UN safe haven Potocari and later disappeared as a result of the fall of Srebrenica. So that's the primary line of information that gave rise to the original list that we have provided. We have additionally, however, done cross-checking of this list, and the second component that relates to how people get on this list that is in vast, vast majority of the cases consistent with the previous issue that I mentioned, which is where the families are reported missing, is where the sample was recovered from. So all but 177 cases listed in that list that I gave come from recovery sites considered by the ICTY to be associated with the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The process of reduction and exclusion, has it been completed? Can we say that the names that we have now are the names that we have? That that's it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- in -- for the most part, I would say yes. If I remember, I made reference yesterday to 11 names that were on a previous list that the ICMP, through its cross-checking, removed from the list, that we consider no longer to be associated with Srebrenica, and we discussed yesterday some of the considerations that went into that. We continue to make identifications and -- and cross-check this information and we haven't found any additional ones for about a year now. So I would suspect that the list that we have presently, absent new identifications that we undoubtedly will make, won't change.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to read out to you your reply from page 77 of yesterday's transcript and I will read it out in English. It will be interpreted for other participants: "[In English] This is a list of DNA match reports that have been issued by the ICMP from the period of November 2001 to August 2011 representing DNA match reports considered by the ICMP to be related to the fall of Srebrenica in 1995." [Interpretation] Did you receive the information or did you yourself establish it, linking the DNA match reports and the events of Srebrenica 1995? "[In English] Considered by the ICMP."

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I made use of the words "considered by the ICMP to be related to the fall of Srebrenica," the basis of that consideration was the explanation that I just gave for how the names got on that list. So that is what I meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Do we then -- should we then understand that your position is that those DNA profiles that you established and linked to the events in Srebrenica in 1995, should we understand -- or can you tell us whether you have established the manner of their death?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The manner of death has been established in a very, very large number of those cases by the pathologists in question. But the manner of death played no role in the establishment of this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that the indictment here, one of the charges is unlawful killings and executions. So is it your claim that those people whose DNA profiles you have established were killed in an unlawful manner and did you separate that from those who were killed in action?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ICMP does not concern itself with whether -- with the legal question of how these people were killed or -- particularly with whether their deaths were lawful or not. I'm reporting on the identifications that have been made with regard to mortal remains recovered from these graves. Now the ICMP has performed a great deal of work with regard to excavations of these sites, and -- and the evidence that was recovered there and much of which is -- has been covered in previous trials and, as I understand it, roughly also with regard to this, there's a lot of evidence that goes to whether or not -- to the circumstances under which these people lost their lives. But, of course, the DNA matches themselves don't indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now briefly be shown 65 ter -- or, rather, P4642. That is the latest list, and it was admitted into evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this not what we saw through Sanction yesterday? Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it appears to be. I also just want to confirm that it's not being broadcast at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now be shown number 9944, please. 9944. This is the sequential number, 9944.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you need to specify what sheet we should look in. There are several sheets, as you know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe we are there. Well, now we have this ordered alphabetically. Could you please bear with me, because I'm looking at a different list. I have the list of 2008. But I would like to be shown --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I -- Mr. Vanderpuye or Mr. Reid, I take it as a spreadsheet it should have a search function.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you search 9944 and -- is it by Mr. Stevanovic or Mr. Reid, I don't know. This is run by Mr. Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have it. We have it. It's the fourth from the bottom. I won't read out the name, but this name under 9944, I don't see if you can see the number, but this is the third or fourth from the bottom. Now could we see the following columns now. Here it says -- well, we see that Bratunac is mentioned. Could we move further to the right, please. The Federal Commission, where we see jurisdiction. Could we move further on. We see the date, 11th July, and then forest, "suma."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us with authority about this victim? Is this a victim that would be included in this indictment?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ICMP does not concern itself with who is and is not included in the indictment. But you also asked me what I can tell you - I think you said with certainty - about this victim. I'm going to make sure that I'm looking at the right -- can you please specify again the line in question? Because you made reference to reassociation and the one I thought you were talking about is a main case, as far as I can tell, on line 9944.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite possible. It is probably my error. Yes, main case. We see the columns: Forest, 11th of July, 1995. What can this Trial Chamber conclude based on this list? Or, rather, this name that's mentioned on the list.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That his remains were recovered from the site listed here, submitted to the ICMP for DNA testing, matched against a database of all -- family references of all missing people -- persons in Bosnia, and found to match a family that had reported this named individual as missing from the fall of Srebrenica in 1995 and having been part of the column of men that departed through the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where was this body recovered?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I just don't recall. I think it says here Bratunac, but I'm not able to provide you with additional information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at the time. Excellencies, should we continue with our questioning or, rather, would we go on break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted, before we broke or moved on from this -- from this screen and this exhibit, that we maybe go into private session and put on the record the name of the individual concerned so there's no confusion later on. I know that Dr. Karadzic has indicated the row number, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The second thing Mr. President is, as with respect this individual and all others, there is a column in this spreadsheet that indicates the site code which would suggest where the body or the body part was recovered. And also the site co-ordinates. So if that's an issue, we can certainly clear that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. We will take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now look again at 9944 to establish what mass grave it was recovered from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps can you help us, Dr. Parsons. Could we see the column showing the site. Is that B Liplje? What is that a reference to? Is it under case ID or -- could you tell us which column would show the mass grave from which the remains were recovered?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The column case ID number with BLIP, which undoubtedly stands for Liplje, would give us one indication. The site code is typically representative of the location it comes from. The site name is another column here. Where it is listed as Bratunac, that would be the most specific information that I would be able to provide looking at this. And to be honest with you, I don't know the site codes and I can't tell you where this came from right now. This list is a condensed list representing general information that we have. There is additional information regarding precisely where this came from, but I don't have any more information that I'm looking at here, and I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we move to the right so that we can see the remaining column. Slowly. Yes. And further. H ... Move it to the right, yes. Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell the Trial Chamber what "main case" actually means?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Main case" would be the first instance with which we've made a match to this particular missing person, as opposed to a reassociation case which would -- when a subsequent body part was found that was also identified to the same individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Looking at 9944 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, with respect to this item, the site code is empty. Do you agree? You said we can find it at that column.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In this instance, it is empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, should the Trial Chamber infer from this that 9944 was killed in July 1995, buried -- or, rather, recovered from a mass grave, D so-and-so. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was reported missing by his family in association with the fall of Srebrenica in 1995, yes. And that's the indication of the site where he was recovered from. I can assure the Court that more specific information concerning that site exists. It is simply not listed in this brief summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we leave this as it is, but briefly take a look at 65 ter 4418. Please bear this one particular case, 9944, in mind. Perhaps you can jot down the elements. We'll get back to it later. But, for now, can we take a look at 4418. 65 ter 4418.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us bear in mind we do not broadcast all the ICMP report out of abundance of caution. Probably we need to switch to e-court from Sanction. I think this is also a CD. All we see is a surrogate sheet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now be shown 1308.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that this is the same person?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the information I'm looking at right now and the corresponding birth date, I would not contest that this is the same individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we take a look at the other columns --

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me. Pardon me, I very much apologise. I did not cross-correlate to what appeared to be a newspaper article that was up. I wasn't answering with respect to that, if that's what the question was. I was merely looking at the -- what appears to be a new Excel sheet and confirming that the information on that Excel sheet seemed to match the information on the previous one I had seen. I'm not sure if the question was posed with relation to the newspaper article or whatever that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So can we have the answer one more time, then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I need the question again. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The victim, under number 1308, is that the same person that we saw earlier on that list, under number 9944? Can you see it? You can see the name, the date of birth, and then we see BLIP 1. And then perhaps if we can be shown the other columns because this list might be more exhaustive. First of all, can we agree this is the same person, because we see it's the same first name, last name, and date of birth. And also there is a reference to Liplje there. As well as Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly appears to be. The critical thing that would indicates that this is, in fact, the very same match report being listed twice would be the protocol numbers and ID numbers, and I forgot to note those. But I have no doubt that this relates to the same DNA match report for the same individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now scroll to the right and see if there's any additional information on this person. We see the date when he went missing. That too is consistent. And then it says forest, so in other words, that's where he disappeared, and then main case. So this database has the same type of information. Would it be necessary to have more information in order for this Trial Chamber to establish that these remains were recovered from a mass grave that is associated with July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This list certainly doesn't constitute an evidentiary record that is clear and complete with regard to what other information may be known that would link this to a grave and, in fact, that grave to the larger event of the fall of Srebrenica and the associated mass killings and formation of clandestine graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this cannot be used as evidence; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "[In English] This list certainly doesn't constitute an evidentiary record that is clear and complete with regard to the other information may be known that would link this to a grave and, in fact, that grave to the larger event of the fall of Srebrenica and the associated mass killings and the formation of clandestine graves." [Interpretation] Can you explain, then, what this list can be used for. What is it that the Trial Chamber can conclude based on this list?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That an individual reported as missing from the fall of Srebrenica was definitively identified by DNA from this particular grave-site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it is one of those 6.006 [as interpreted] persons that you were able to identify; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can the Trial Chamber, based on your findings, establish that this person was a victim of an execution?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very possibly by examining the specific records in association with this case, to go to the excavation findings of the site where the body was recovered, to go to the autopsy report and anthropology findings, and to consider the DNA linkages between different graves that indicate their causal association one with another, this entire body of evidence could certainly be brought to bear in any one of these cases and very possibly answer exactly the question that you posed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would that be a conservative conclusion or a liberal one? What could be established beyond a reasonable doubt that this person was a victim of execution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's not for the witness to tell that to the Chamber. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would also add that Dr. Karadzic seems to be proceeding along an assumption with respect to this particular individual. Dr. Parsons indicates these mortal remains were recovered in a number of different contexts, some relating to mass graves, secondary graves, fragmented body parts, surface remains included. So we seem to be proceeding along the presumption that this particular individual is a victim of an execution resulting in -- is -- his mortal remains being deposited in a mass grave and that is not clear, first of all, from the evidence in question as it stands now. And so I don't think that that is an appropriate means to -- an appropriate way of questioning the witness since the circumstances under which the recovery of these mortal remains are not clear from the record or from the exhibit that's in front of him now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic, having heard Mr. Vanderpuye's intervention?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, my question is this: How can the Trial Chamber use the findings of your report? This list is the product of your work. So what can the Trial Chamber conclude based on it? Is it what you've just said a moment ago, that that person was identified as no longer living, and perhaps also that it was -- that its remains were recovered from some mass grave; correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm exceptionally hesitant to make statements regarding what the Trial Chamber could and could not conclude. I don't know what other evidence has been presented to the Court and that is the area of the Trial Chamber. I'm sorry, I can't do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely. Dr. Parsons said that what he can conclude from this is, line 23 to line 25, on page 35: "... that an individual reported as missing from the fall of Srebrenica was definitely identified by DNA from this particular grave-site." Yes, please move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have from this list number 1740. Yes. We find it twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did this repetition come about, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would ask, please, that we could scroll to the right. And further, please. I guess we have to continue. There we go. Two different parts of this individual were recovered separately and separately identified by DNA because they had been dissociated in the process of the creation of a clandestine secondary mass grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the column C, third column? The one below has an additional letter, R. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That R indicates that it is a reassociation of a different sample from the same individual as the preceding case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that tells that one is main case and the other reassociation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we note this person down as well. So, for the time being, we have two people, or two numbers. 1308 and 1740. Could we have next 2403. Doctor, would you prefer to see the other list or is this one more complete?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure which list this is. I apologise. Is this the one that was received just the other day, this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. This one is from 2008 and the other one came a bit later. I thought the previous, the earlier one, may have more elements that may assist you in identifying where and where from the remains arrived.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. The most recent list would be the most informative list to be using, but I'm comfortable with the information that is on this list as well. If you have particular questions relating to it, it's fine with me to use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What do you conclude or how do you interpret the location of the remains under this number, 2403 to 2405? Where were they found, how they ended up there, and what are they associated with?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry that I don't have site codes memorised, so I can't tell you definitively where these came from. I noticed that the -- the prefix in each of the sample numbers, B.KAM.BR are all the same and that indicates to me that they came from the same grave that would have been associated with a general locality known as Kamenica. Also, I happen to know that's an alternative name for the Cancari road series of secondary mass graves. So how -- if I am correct in that and I'm quite confident that I am, then I would say that these remains came to be in this grave-site because they were brought there by the perpetrators of the death of these individuals and buried in that site sometime in the fall of 1995, after having been previously buried in a different primary grave-site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we note down this number too or keep these elements in mind. Next, could we have 2743 from the same list. What can be said about this body or this set of remains, in addition to the date of birth, starting from column C and further?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This apparently comes from one of the Liplje secondary mass graves and the date of birth would be as listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can anything else can be concluded? Was it found in a mass grave, is it a mass grave location?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not prepared to indicate that I can give you definitive information about these particular grave-sites, but I don't want to dissemble either, and I will tell you based on this code it looks very much like it is a Liplje grave, Liplje 04, which, if I remember correctly, is a secondary grave associated with the primary execution site of the Petkovici dam by DNA linkages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we take note of this case too, the elements concerning this person. Then we should move to 8623 on the same list. So we have 2, 3, 4, 5. You see that there are two possible names. Can you tell us where this body was collected? Is it Lazete 2B?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm hesitant to appear definitive with regard to these site codes and their locations, but that would certainly be what I understand from looking at this. The highly probable correct answer is that, yes, it is from Lazete grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we note down this case too. Can we then go to 3670 to 3673. Can you tell us pretty much the same thing regarding this name? You can interpret the findings of your institution, of course. What does all this mean?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would appear that these series of remains were recovered from Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't insist on further individual examples. Let us try to sum it up. Dr. Parsons, did you know that in the area where these bodies were extracted, the war went on for 44 months. There were many casualties who were buried in mass graves before July 1995. Did you know about this category of people who were killed before the 10th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I am aware that people were killed throughout the course of the war and it wouldn't surprise me to discover that they had been buried. That's an extremely general statement. You've asked me to comment on this. Are you suggesting that bodies were collected over the 44 months of the year and then around July 11th, 1995, all these bodies that had been collected were deposited into large primary mass graves and then, for whatever reason, subsequently exhumed and buried in a series of secondary mass graves? Is that the scenario you're trying to suggest that I respond to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, but I will put a scenario to you. It is as follows. As of April 1992 until April 1993, there was daily intensive fighting. The burial of enemy casualties took place on the spot, for the most part. Later on, during the sanitation and hygiene measures procedures, following some other fighting, other casualties were buried there. As of April 1993 until July 1994, there was less fighting. There was fighting against sabotage groups and fighting expeditions and incursions into Serb territory. The casualties which took place then were buried in smaller or larger mass graves. In July 1995 -- well, let me ask you this first: Do you accept that it could have been as I put it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a general statement, yes. But with regard to the cases that you just walked me through, that would not be consistent with my understanding of those sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that in the second week of July 1995, there were victims due to fighting between the column and the Serb army, as well as mutual fighting amongst the Muslims in the column? There were victims of minefields. Does this finding of yours, does this report differentiate between the types of victims so as to know who were the victims of executions?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the cases that we've walked through so far, based on the information that you asked me about and that I saw here, indicate that these are related to a number of well-documented large primary execution events and very large primary mass graves that resulted from that. Of course, I consider it reasonable that some individuals were killed en route and died in multiple circumstances with regard to the column that attempted to escape from Srebrenica, but none -- none of these are, for example, surface remains that -- that have been recovered from that environment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the transcript page 22677. It is the testimony of Witness 045.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You will see, Doctor, that all these people, or all these remains, were found in a number of mass graves but were killed in a single location in the presence of the witness whose testimony we will look into, and as a result of combat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why do we have to show a testimony of protected witness to Dr. Parsons? Why don't you just put it to ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask that we see one page. It doesn't need to be broadcast. This is where we have the names identified by first name, father's name, and the witness confirmed that he saw it with his own eyes, those people being killed in fighting. There were no executions, especially not in a single location, and the people were not buried in a single location. The same witness said that they left their dead and carried away their wounded, and the Serbs buried the dead later on. This is a very illustrative page, and I would kindly ask that we see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Shall we -- that -- I have to confer with the Registrar whether it was examined in private session. Then we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we upload the spreadsheet? 65 ter number 4418. Or Mr. Vanderpuye can help us, whether you do not challenge the names referred to are the same ones appearing in the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is no challenge, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you proceed on that basis, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we would be wise to get going and if we need to do further cross-correlation we could do that. I, of course, don't know anything about the witness that was quoted in the most recent document we've seen, but one of the things that I think would be necessary for us to keep in mind with regard to this issue is the true identity of the individuals who were named by that witness in comparison to the individuals on the list of DNA match reports, notwithstanding that they have the same names. It's quite remarkable, the -- how frequent names are in the Bosnian Muslim population. Very, very many people share the same first name and the same last name, and because the first names are very common, people actually share the same father's name as well. I happened to look into this recently. We have in our missing persons database 25.000 different missing persons represented. Fully 2.000 of those individuals share the same first and last name. And we have 83 incidences where the -- of different individuals saying -- sharing the same first name, the same last name, and the same father's name. So I would not be prepared to jump to the conclusion that even if these names appear the same, that they actually refer to the same individual. And if you look at the -- list of DNA match reports that these -- that this series of names were pulled out of, I noticed in many of the instances that there were scores of individuals in the Srebrenica missing persons list that had, for example, the same last name as the individual in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us put it in a somewhat different perspective, Doctor. Among those 6.600, approximately, persons identified, you would not exclude a possibility that there are some victims or there are some persons who died not as a result of execution, whatever its ratio may be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I would agree with that statement. But I also think it's likely that within this set of 6.600, or certainly within the larger number of people involved in the Srebrenica event, that there might be people that share the same first, last, and father's name, and I'm not convinced based on what I've seen that the individuals referred to by the witness are actually the same individuals that were highlighted in the Excel sheet. It is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Had two men got killed, I mean, the first two on this list who have the same name and surname and the same father, how would you identify them? Would there be two profiles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. And then as long as we do not mention those specific names and then we do not show the transcript page, we can go back to open session. Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we in public session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. We are still in private session. So shall we go back to open session? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry that we were in closed session. I don't think any of has to be redacted. It is only the names that don't have to displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now let me ask you this, Dr. Parsons, in view of everything that you said, that perhaps these are some other people with the same names and surnames and the same father's name. If we had two such names, would you identify both of them and would we have a different DNA profile?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.
