They would be identified genetically, not with regard to names, because we could see the relationships that each of these different individuals would have to their specific family members. So we have many instances of DNA match reports with the same person's name on them but with different ICMP ID numbers that relate to different people. And, yes, you are correct, they would have different DNA profiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I were to put it to you that in your list of identified DNA profiles there are no duplicates, as far as these persons are concerned, is it probable that these were the same persons from this witness 's testimony? Or, rather, that that's on the rise.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a hard time commenting on that probability because I don't know -- like this witness, I don't know what would have happened to the remains of the individuals he was referring to, and so I really don't know the probability with which those individuals would have made their way into the grave-sites that were in question in the list. I will admit it is a possibility that bears consideration. And you said if you were to put to me that there is no one in the list that has those duplications, that's an if. I don't know that that's the case and I would be a little bit surprised if it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question is, since we have not found anywhere in the list any other names, except from these, with these fathers, and we find them in the testimony as well, is it then probable that these are one and the same persons? Is that very likely, because there are no duplicates with different DNAs?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You state that. I don't -- I don't know the basis upon which you've done that search or -- or have any reason to have confidence in that statement. It may well be true; I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Vanderpuye, if you could scroll back your transcript page. From page 47 of today, from line 3, I think we can redact the confidentiality of -- of those parts of the transcript. From then on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be done. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, we can do that through a search, all of us here. In your very own documents, there are no other persons with this name and surname and father's name, and they appear in testimony as well. How can there be any doubt in our minds as to whether these are one and the same persons, when, in your list, there are no other persons with the same DNA?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have you searched the ICMP ID numbers and compared -- okay. First of all, there were in the list we were seeing numerous entries with the same first name, last name, and father's name. And then the question is whether these would have different ICMP ID numbers or not, and I don't know the answer to that question. I'm not trying to be obtuse, it could be well be what you say is true, but I'm skeptical that it's been checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think you've exhausted this issue. We can move on. Your time is limited. And I should have said "lift the confidentiality" instead of "redacting the confidentiality."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can you tell the Trial Chamber briefly what are STR markers and what is their role in all of this that you did?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: STR markers is a generic name for the type of genetic loci that are used in these identifications. STR stands for short tandem repeat. And these are short elements of DNA within everyone's genome. The genome is the total collection of DNA that you have. And the short tandem repeat part of it refers to small blocks of DNA letters, A, G, C and T, normally in quadruplets that are repeated different numbers of times. So what that corresponds to is a locus or a particular place on the DNA which is the STRs are, so the STR locus is a particular place on the DNA, and that locus is highly variable between individuals in the population, having to do with the number of these little repeat units that are in there. Now, so, in -- in one individual chromosome you may have -- actually let me go back. Another thing I need to add is that everyone has two copies of their DNA, so we have paired chromosomes with copies of DNA, one that you got from your mother and one that you got from your father. So for each locus, which is the word we're using that corresponds to these STR markers, everybody has two different copies, but each of those copies may have a different number of these little short tandem repeats in them. So what that means is when you check the DNA at these different loci and see how many repeats an individual has in each of his two copies, one from the mother and one from the father, you can very quickly distinguish individuals one from the other. Now, these different loci -- loci simply means a position. I've used that word a few times and I'm going to try to use it consistently. Each of these STR markers exists at a different locus, a different position on the chromosome, and each one of those is independent of the other ones. So using the type of test that we do standardly, we investigate 15 different independent STR loci, each one of which is highly variable. So it is by comparing the number of repeats in each of the two copies everyone has at each of these 15 locations that we develop a DNA profile that can be considered as unique to an individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that on the basis of STR markers, nothing can be concluded about that particular person except for the fact that that is person? You cannot establish that the person had been ill, you cannot establish what that person's health was, you cannot establish that person's ethnicity, none of that. Am I right when I say that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In broad stroke, yes. And for the practical purposes of this courtroom, what you said is correct. I will add that one thing you can tell is who this individual is related to. So it's not just his identity, but his identity relative to his family members also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it necessary then to code these findings established in STR or expressed in STR, and what is the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these STR markers are the same markers that are used in a large number of different types of databases worldwide. One of them is a criminal offender databases that are maintained by many, many countries. So it has been recognised in the European Court of Human Rights and various other places that this type of information should be considered private and sensitive. It is a unique identifier, and if you have someone's DNA profile, you can establish your own database, potentially, and use it for your own purposes, whatever those may be. That mere fact alone is the kind of thing that has caused widespread concern in today's societies with regard to the protection of genetic information, who has access to it, and how you may be identified. In the contexts of this missing persons activity and the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, we have families that have been traumatised by the loss of their loved ones and the overall impact -- the shattering impact of war. They're extremely psychologically affected and they want to have their loved ones back. Very important to them. In order to do so we need to obtain genetic samples from them, but we don't want to have to tell them that in order to get their loved one back not only do they have to give us their DNA, but that we will happily turn it over to the individuals that they consider complicit in the death of their family members. So that would be the primary reason why we would maintain that information as confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that information confidential for the pathologist who provided the material? Why is coded information being sent to him as well?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the word has been used in this courtroom which is abundance of caution. I -- more or less a need to know basis. In fact the pathologists don't do anything useful with the real genetic data that they couldn't do with the coded genetic data, and so to prevent the occurrence of that DNA match report falling out the window and blowing down the street and thereby allowing somebody else to have access to it, we have instead included coded information which in no means compromises the identification process. Many DNA laboratories in the United States and elsewhere that report official DNA findings do not include DNA profiles at all on their DNA match reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If a family would like to check ICMP data, what would the proper course of action be; and would it be possible, to begin with?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We haven't encountered that situation very much. We consider that the DNA profile and biological sample that the family member have provided to the ICMP to be essentially their property. So as I said, we haven't encountered this very much, but I believe that if a family member were to ask, we would provide them with their DNA profile. We would not, I think, provide them with the DNA profiles of other family members, and as you're aware, or as has been mentioned previously in this courtroom, in fact this DNA data can provide information regarding the relationships of family members that may be different than one or more of the family members understand them to be. These nuclear STR markers, for example, are the standard method by which DNA paternity testings are conducted, and if a family were -- if an individual were to come to us with a paternity question with relation to the samples that had been provided to the ICMP, we would not provide that information. In other words, we would not provide information about any other individual than that person. If an entire family came to us and said, We would like our profiles, each of them individually requesting, we would individually hand them over and they would be free to compare them if they wish. Again, I'll say we have not encountered this situation. Although I think we have got one or two inquiries related to paternity kind of issues that we have declined to release information for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But can the family not draw any conclusions on the basis of the coded formulas as well?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, theoretically they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I'm interested in now: How can I be sure that you have 6.600 unique profiles in your base? Am I supposed to take your word for it or do I have a way of verifying this?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mechanism for verification that ICMP has proposed as early as 2009 is to provide to you a random and representative selection of ICMP case files containing all information that you're able to review and -- and -- and test their authenticity and accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You certainly know that we asked for five, according to our own choice, and 295 random samples. And out of the five we only got four. We haven't received the fifth one yet. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you this, please: We agreed that the probability would have been slightly lower had you taken into account 29.000, right, instead of 7.000?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about CLR? Actually, can you tell the Trial Chamber what CLR is? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We may have some kind of a communication problem. I don't know what CLR is. You may be talking about VLR. Does that sound correct? LR standing for likelihood ratio. And that is one of the statistics included in our conclusion statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Maybe in our language it's called something different. It should be combined likelihood ratio. Does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The ICMP doesn't refer to it as a combined likelihood ratio but we refer to it simply as the likelihood ratio. But I'm confident we're talking about the same thing. And, no, the estimate of the prior probability does not have an effect on the likelihood ratio. That's independent of the circumstances of the case, which the prior odds are dependent upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So had you taken 29.000 or 30.000 missing persons instead of 7.000, you said that the probability would have decreased to a certain degree. Is that correct that you use a population base database that pertains to all of the former Yugoslavia? Is that what you use in your research?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In order to calculate the statistics that we use, you have to know how common these different STR types are in the general population and it is then common practice to use a population reference database. And the one that we use is representative of the overall constituency of the Bosnian population representing some of each of the ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For example, when calculating probability if you had not taken, say, these 29.000 but the population base of the former Yugoslavia, would the coefficient of probability be even lower? Would that approach have been even more conservative?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to have to request that you repeat your question. I didn't catch exactly the "if" part of it. If what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For example, when calculating probability in Srebrenica you took 1 to 7.000. We agreed that had you taken 30.000 instead of 7.000, the ratio would have been somewhat lower. Would it have been even lower had you taken 2.900.000 Muslims, the population base of Muslims or the population base of all of Yugoslavia? The one that you use -- the one that you refer to, rather.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I doubt it would change significantly at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it would introduce a change, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Potentially a very small change in some of the final digits. But I will say that it doesn't mean that the change is uniformly going to be lower. It could very well increase the statistics just as easily with this minor fluctuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whatever. Why didn't you take the population base of the Muslims, 2.900.000?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a bit expensive to test 2 million people when the database can serve adequately and completely correctly with a much smaller sample size.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Had you been told that one of these victims was not a victim from Srebrenica from July 1995, would your statistics look different?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't get the interpretation. My -- my head phone was out of order. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would please ask that the -- I'm struggling for the sense of the question and maybe if it were repeated again, I could understand it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would the prior probability be different if you had been told that there were victims there who were not victims from the second week of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would change the prior probability is the number of individuals missing in a particular region or event that -- that gives rise to our expectation of finding an individual within that -- within that pool of victims. So I think -- I guess theoretically the answer to your question is yes, but I can't answer it in a very systematic manner. If we feel that there are a certain number of victims pertaining to a particular area, in other words, that if we pick up a set of remains what's the total number of individuals that this could relate to, we -- we take our estimate, our best estimate of the number of missing from that region or event and use that. If we had a different understanding of that number, we would use a different number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So something had to be presumed there, that these were victims from the second week of July 1995 and that they were victims of an execution. And that was quite a determining factor for you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of whether they were executed versus killed in combat or what have you, no, that wouldn't affect the possibility. Again, cause and manner of death doesn't have anything to do with the identification of the -- of the individual. But if we thought there were a substantially different number of people involved, we would have been wise to use a different number. I will note that having now identified almost 7.000 people from this region -- so we have done the experiment, we're recovered bodies, we've seen how many individuals there are there, and I think the number of 6.772 is quite similar to the prior probability of 1 in 7.000 that we did, so I have very little concern that we have much of a problem here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it your position that all of these 6.000-something persons were victims from July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not my position that they all were, but I would say it's my position that the vast majority of them are. 5.354 of them can be related to one of the five primary large graves or assemblages of large secondary mass graves for which there exists a vast amount of evidence regarding their formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever been told what happened with the people who were killed before July 1995 and where they were buried?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can also not distinguish between victims of executions and combat victims if we remain with the second week of July 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are asking repetitive questions. It's time to conclude your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, if I can use the remaining time before the break, I will complete my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Mr. Karadzic, you passed your time long ago. How long would you need for your re-examination, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have a re-direct examination planned for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Continue, Mr. Karadzic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the population of Srebrenica was before the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it is not for the witness to tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, on page 79 you said "men and boys." What do you mean by "boys"? What is your definition of "boys"? Is that your own definition or is that something that you actually took over from the indictment or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will confess that that is language that has lapsed into common usage and I suppose I didn't have anything highly specific in mind. I have seen from the Podrinje identification project age distributions of the identified victims and there are people that -- within that that would certainly be considered minors. So if you would press me now, I might say below 18. And there are certainly enough individuals in that age range that would be -- if I adopt that as a definition, that it would be proper to refer to the -- the victims as being men and boys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you then define the word "boys" in your own understanding?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. Let me pick, 18 years and younger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Muslim side regularly recruited men between the ages of 16 and 59?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Also it is not for the witness to testify about that. Let us conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what was the extent of your co-operation with this OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have been asked to provide summary records such as have been entered into evidence here. That's our predominant interaction. I will say that we've spent a great deal of time over the years interacting with the Office of the Prosecutor in attempting to negotiate with your team the simple expedient of providing a random and representative sample of case files for your Defence review. That would be another area where we've had a lot of interactions. But everything that we have in -- interacted with the OTP with, with regard to this Tribunal, I think has been perfectly apparent in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I then ask you why you refused to meet with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I thought -- I felt like the extensive interactions that we were already having with you through the OTP would more than suffice for -- for our interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What interests do you have? What are they?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To provide to this Court an objective record of what the ICMP's findings have been that are considered relevant to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if you consider them relevant to the Defence as well, why did you refuse to meet with the Defence? Or is it, rather, your position that they're only relevant for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First, I think Dr. Parsons has already answered the question directly and also implicitly in a number of ways. The second thing I wanted to point out is that there appears to an error in the transcript with respect to one of his answers at page 59, lines 19 through 20. And in -- in that line, Dr. Parsons stated that he had very little concern that there was much of a problem and that concerned the use of prior odds. It's recorded incorrectly in the transcript. If necessary, perhaps he can -- he can restate that answer. So I just wanted to bring that to the attention of the Court, in addition to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Also, Mr. President, I've noticed that the witness has not had the LiveNote access. He just -- both of his monitors are in e-court so it's maybe made it more difficult for him to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, do you confirm that Mr. Vanderpuye just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't -- if you're referring to a previous statement that was incorrectly transcribed, I'm not familiar. I would have to look at it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you -- could you ask -- Mr. Vanderpuye, could you confirm with the witness as to what you brought up earlier on. Page 59, lines 19 to 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Yes. In response to a question that was put to you by Dr. Karadzic, the question was: "So something had to be presumed there, that these were victims from the second week of July 1995 and that they were victims of an execution. And that was quite a determining factor for you, wasn't it?" And your answer was: "With regard to the issue of whether they were executed versus killed in combat, or what have you, no. That went" -- I think it should read "wouldn't," but it says "that went affect the possibility. Again, cause and manner of death doesn't have anything to do with the identification of the individual. But if we thought there were a substantially different number of people involved, we would have been wise to use a different number. "I will note that having now identified almost 7.000 people from this region -- so we have done the -- so we've done the experiment, we've recovered bodies, I think the number of 6.772 is quite similar to the prior probability of 1 in 7.000." And then reads: "So I have a concern that we don't have very much of a problem here," and there's an indication that there was some part of your answer there that was not recorded. So the question is: In relation to the last part of your answer, if you could restate it so the record is clear that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification. I meant to say based on the similarity between 6.772 and 7.000, that I don't have a concern with regard to the use of the value 1 in 7.000 as a prior probability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. I remember he said "little concern." Yes, Mr. Karadzic, where were we? It's time to conclude. And you just asked a repetitive question, but I would allow you to wrap it up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Parsons, you were not an expert witness before any other court. Can we agree that you are a participant in these proceedings, and that your position on the possible suspiciousness of the findings should be carefully balanced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, it's not for the witness to testify about that. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was going to register my objection but I also wanted to ask leave of the Court to ask one question on redirect examination. As I believe that Dr. Karadzic is about to conclude, I thought I would bring that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you, Mr. Parsons, whether you understand the significance of certain unclarities and doubts about the findings. Are you aware what their effect on these proceedings are and do you realise that all these doubts and discrepancies are very important for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what doubts and discrepancies you refer to. That is such a wide-ranging set of statements that I can't provide a useful answer. I certainly have a strong sense of the way forensic evidence fits together in combination to provide an overall picture. And I have a great deal of confidence in this courtroom to evaluate the significance, and I hope the objective presentation of the findings of the ICMP will help them to reach those conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just one question, Dr. Parsons. At page 56, lines 4 through 7, Dr. Karadzic mentioned that the Defence had requested some five case files in addition to some 295 randomly selected ones. He asked you whether you were aware that the Defence had only received four of the five specifically selected files. Can you tell us -- you indicated that you were aware of that. Can you tell us why the Defence hasn't received all five of these files as yet?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is a very involved process to reach out to the family members to request consent, and then, of course, it is up to them to determine whether they want to comply with that consent request. In this instance, the fifth of the five families has not yet been able to fill out the consent forms and -- and take part in the process. They live in different parts of Europe. It's simply communications. It's my understanding that -- that they will provide consent, but prior to them having done so, I'm not prepared to assume that they will, but our understanding is that they will.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions on re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless my colleagues have questions for you, Doctor, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber, as well as the Tribunal as a whole, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it again, and now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we rise, the Chamber grants the Prosecution motion to amend its Rule 65 ter witness list filed on 20th of March, 2012, which the Defence did not oppose, and orders that the Prosecution file a revised 65 ter witness list of witnesses reflecting these amendments no later than Monday, 26th of March, 2012. We'll break for an hour and resume at 1.35. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'd like to put something on the record relating to a witness who testified in closed session. So we may go into private session for that for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, Mr. President. I just wanted to address one quick housekeeping matter while that was taking place. Yesterday, at transcript pages 21482 through 84, the Trial Chamber inquired about an English translation for 65 ter 21043 which is now marked for identification as P4645. I simply wanted to advise the Court that a translation is available, and if the exhibit is released by the Registry, it can be uploaded and we seek to admit it in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be done. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Could I tender the document that we received from the witness about the countries supporting ICMP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I -- is there any opposition, Mr. Tieger? Did you follow the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not to a large extent but I think that that -- because there was discussion between Mr. Robinson and Mr. Vanderpuye, I think I'd prefer to inquire before I simply acquiesced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think -- excuse me. Personally I understand that that's the information available from the web site of that organisation. So we shall admit -- we will admit it and give a number. But could you -- why don't you take a look at that -- that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't have any reason at the moment to think there's a problem, but it seems likely it's the appropriate thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll wait for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, madam. Could you take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Witness. Can we begin by having you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: My name is Teufika Ibrahimefendic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Ms. Ibrahimefendic, is it correct that you have testified before this Tribunal on three previous occasions, in the Tolimir case in February of 2011; in the Plavsic case in December 2002; and particularly, in the case of Prosecutor versus Krstic on the 27th of July, 2000?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that you had the opportunity to review your testimony in the Krstic case. Bearing in mind that that related to what was known in the year 2000, do you confirm that the Krstic testimony accurately reflects your evidence before that Court, that it was truthful, and if you were asked about the same matters here, you would provide the same information to the Court. That is, you stand by your testimony in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender 65 ter 03261, the Krstic testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that would be admitted as the next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4646, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ms. Ibrahimefendic, I will now read a very brief summary of your testimony in the Krstic case so that the public can know generally what that was about. The witness is a psychotherapist who has worked with women and children traumatised by war. Since 1994 she has worked for Vive Zene, a multi-disciplinary organisation specialising in the treatment of victims of war, including hundreds of women and children traumatised by the July 1995 events in Srebrenica. The witness testified about the effects of the trauma on the Srebrenica victims, including various forms of emotional and behavioural damage. Witness, that concludes the summary and I have just a few additional questions for you. First, I want to quickly cover some of your experiences since you testified in the Krstic case. Is it correct that you have continued as a psychotherapist at Vive Zene and are currently the co-ordinator of the education and training programme?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that since the year 2000, you have continued to work in the field of trauma treatment, that you have specialised as a trauma treatment specialist, including conducting trainings for other professionals, for researchers, for investigators, law enforcement officials and so on?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I am the co-ordinator of the education team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And beyond your management and training responsibilities, have you carried an active case-load yourself, which, in fact, takes up the bulk of your professional time?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Most of my time, about 60 per cent, goes on my work with people who were victims of trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you are a member of the European Association for Psychotherapists and of the European Association of Gestalt Psychotherapy experts?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. As of 2004, I am a member of the European Association of Gestalt Psychotherapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, is it correct that you have worked with Serb victims of war as well as Bosniaks victims?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I worked with Serb victims, people who suffered losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few questions in connection with your Krstic testimony. At page 5814 of your Krstic testimony, you spoke about the exceptionally high level of trauma experienced by the Srebrenica survivors and the various effects of that trauma on their lives. And at page 5824, you referred to the fact that this was not a natural disaster which made it even more traumatic. I wanted, therefore, to ask you: With respect to the effect of events involving the loss of family members, is there a difference between so-called normal or conventional losses and traumatic loss?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: In the course of a life, each individual goes through a developmental period, period of maturation and then of aging, and throughout life, everyone suffers various losses, and these losses are considered natural, normal losses. For instance, if an adult, 60 years of age, losses a parent who is 80 years old that would be considered a normal loss and such losses may lead to temporary changes, or, rather, require additional adaptation to life. However, after a while, the family and the individual would stabilise and continue on with their life. So there is a big differences between losses that are part of life, as it were, and traumatic losses. Traumatic losses may be the loss of a child, even -- not in war-time circumstances, because it is not normal for a child to die before their parent. Traumatic losses incurred in the course of war are especially stressful because they come out of the blue. They are unpredictable because there are also many cases where the parents lose their children. The children were taken away, or they go missing. In the case of male family members that also had a great impact on the family and the structure of the family, the relationships between the family members, different roles within it, and so on and so forth, and, on the other hand, it also has a major impact on the development of the children. So these traumatic losses are always followed by post-traumatic effects that the survivors have to go through for the rest of their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. You described for the Krstic Trial Chamber about five years after the events of July 1995 some of the effects of the trauma that the victims had suffered, including women who experienced nightmares, depression, apathy, and whose psychological condition was "extremely grave," and children who suffered, depending on their age group, from various effects ranging from nightmares to learning disorders to generalised fears and withdrawal. I'd like to ask you, in light of your continuing work with the victims, if you can tell us whether - and what - effects are still experienced by the victims, as a result of the trauma they experienced, and if it is helpful to break that down into broad categories and then give us some examples from each category, please feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: The consequences as a result of an initial trauma, or perhaps we should say a trauma that starts at the beginning of a war, can be divided into consequences that have to do with the emotional life. There would be consequences of cognitive nature. Then there would be consequences that would have an effect on the physical or that would affect interactions with other people. As for emotional reactions the most frequent consequence is fear, fear that becomes dominant, the fear for oneself and for one's family, the worry about and anxiety about one's own life and the lives of family members, the anxiety about the physical danger and threat. There were also other emotions such as helplessness and loss of control over one's own life. Then there is grief, anger. People were angry. Why was all this happening? Why to them, in particular. Even to this day, there are people who would put this question to me: Why did this happen to me? Why was I there? And then follows the question: Could I have done something else? Could I have done something, taken some measures to save my loved ones, and so on and so forth. So there's a whole range of emotions that are at play. Changes of mood, mood swings, up to the feeling of betrayal, deceit, that there's no other instance that one can have faith in anymore. As for the physical consequences, these have to do with the constant stress of the body. People feel constantly stressed out. They have insomnia problems, problems with eating, transpiration and so on, and they would frequently seek medical assistance in those cases. The behavioural problems also have to do with these people seeking to be alone or else they would establish links and become too dependent on other people. But there would also be effects within families where traumatised members of a family or those who are traumatised to a greater degree tend not to share this with other family members and they disassociate themselves from family members. This would lead to problems with memory, memory loss, decision-making. It becomes very difficult to take any decision. They become rigid and are unable to do things that they used to be able to do. Frequently, there would be flashbacks although they try not to bring up those memories. But they have flashbacks that are involuntary memories of their loss and this would impede their day-to-day functions. But the greatest impact and consequences are in their interactions with other people. These are damaged. People do not trust each other. They do not have the ability to empathise with others so they avoid talking to others about themselves, and especially not with their family members or friends, or their children, because they want to spare their children this trauma. But, in this way, this leads to loss of contacts, and much of this remains hidden away from the rest. And this all leads to various effects on the emotional, cognitive, behavioural, or physical existence which are at the base of such traumatic events. Of course, this has to do -- this is related to the trauma that they have been living through from the very beginning up to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And, finally, I wanted to ask you about a related matter. You've just described some of the continuing effects of the trauma they suffered. I wanted to ask you whether you were able to observe what effect the events of -- the trauma they experienced in July of 1995 and those events had on the normal sources of support to whom people routinely turn when they have experienced traumatic loss.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: When such an extremely traumatic event takes place, if an individual is hurt, and that individual is part of a family, then it affects the whole family. If several members of the family are hurt, the total destruction of the family becomes even greater. Every family is part of a network. If one family is damaged, then a whole -- the whole network of families is damaged. If the network is damaged, the community is damaged. If one thinks about such enormous traumatic events, it means that the entire community is affected by this sorrow, despair and suffering. Under such circumstances, the victims have to fall back on their own resources, and it is typical for the human body to turn on the survival instincts in such circumstances by either fleeing or fighting. In this case they had nowhere to flee, they couldn't go away. And then they focus on their own resources as to how to survive, how to take care of themselves and their loved ones since they felt responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Ibrahimefendic, your evidence in-chief was admitted in lieu of your oral testimony in written form, as you noted. You will now further be asked by Mr. Karadzic in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Ibrahimefendic.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's start with what was said here today, as I'm slightly confused with the way Mr. Tieger was interpreted as well as what you said. You said that you were engaged in the education of the -- those affected by the trauma, whereas it seems that in the interpretation it was interpreted as if you treated them.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I treated the professionals, but I tried to re-educate those affected. The organisation I work for has additional educational channels, from Europe, from a number of different trauma centres. Our entire team is educated to work with the victims of trauma or torture and now we try to disseminate that knowledge in order to help medical professionals to try and cope with the influx and size of problems, as well as the number of people seeking help. Usually such people do not recognise the fact that their problems are related to a trauma or loss but tend to see their problems in a different light.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 72 today, you mentioned that there were normal losses, so to say. Let us try and establish what the category is. Should we call them abnormal or unforeseen or unexpected losses? Which of these alternative or analogous terms would you use?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: As regards traumatic losses I would use what I have. It is unpredictable. It is abnormal. If someone is sick, then, in a way, the family and those close to him or her have time to prepare themselves for the loss of a family member. So it's all I've said. It is unpredictable, abnormal, because it is abnormal for someone to lose 20 family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 73, you continued discussing the phenomena and symptoms. You discussed the consequences on the emotional, cognitive, physical, and interpersonal level.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do such phenomena figure in the general population which had not been traumatised?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: One could say that the number of those who were not touched by trauma is truly very small. Even I am affected as I work with people who have experienced trauma. There are differences, though. Those who carry their anxiety or sorrow related to the war do not share those feelings. They close in and there's this constant feeling that no one can help them. Although, I must say that as of late, more and more people come in seeking help as they realise that they no longer can cope alone and that they have to share it with someone and that they have to face up to what is inside. They become aware of the fact that years have gone by without them being able to forget. As for the normal population, such people tend to share. There is no sense of blame, shame. Perhaps they can feel anger, but such people are more ready to share their feelings and seek help. That's how I see the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correct, then, if I believe that you carried out some research as opposed to the -- a control group in the general population to show specific differences in order to see what the differences are between the people who underwent trauma as opposed to those who did not?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: We did conduct quality research and quantity, although most of it is quality research. We worked with some other organisations as well, including the University of Tuzla and the University of Basel. We had an interdisciplinary research, where also NGOs participated, as well as the University of Basel. They did their quality research, and this is what we would say as to the difference. It is a fact that traumatised people are more susceptible, more prone to depression, more anxious, and that they have other symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder. They have obsessive and compulsive symptoms as opposed to the control group. What prevails very much is the interpersonal level in relationships. There's this high sensitivity in contacts with others, and the quality of life suffers as a consequence. It becomes extremely poor in people who had undergone trauma.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who headed the research project?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: It was headed by the deans and professors of the medical school, as well as the school of rehabilitation, and the Basel school for social welfare, as well as the school for social welfare in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we make use of the results of that research?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Not for the time being, as it was a qualitative research and the data is still being processed. The results for the research I mentioned have more to do with juvenile delinquency, so there will be different aspects that we will study, and for the time being the research has not been completed. We do have a lot of individual cases which we processed and analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do I have to conclude, then, that what you said in the Krstic case and what you have testified so far in this case is not based on the results of that research but based on your impressions?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No. We regularly participate in all conferences in Bosnia-Herzegovina and beyond, and we use the results of research and study conducted by our psychiatrist colleagues, say, in Tuzla. We rely on their results and we test them. A study needn't necessarily be ours but we can still verify it in practice. There are Ph.D. theses on the topic of traumatic and post-traumatic stress disorder as well as Ph.D. theses on the research into missing family members and a comparison with control groups with families which did not miss family members. So all such results are well-known. We mostly deal with treatment, though. All that research is only there to make a diagnosis but we want to treat, and that is our primary goal. In Bosnia, including Republika Srpska, there are no such institutions. There are mental health centres which have only started setting up offices to assist people who had survived the war. In the Federation, there are also mental health centres which are now being equipped to see people with such issues. There is a problem when they go to their local health centre. That is to say, the primary medical system or care. They need to ask for a referral, so they have to travel all this path to meet a person with whom they can discuss their losses and have their trauma recognised and acknowledged so that they would, in turn, would receive respect, pride, faith in people, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But we now have to establish together whether you are testifying based on others' Ph.D. thesis and research or based on your own professional and expert work.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I can testify on the basis of my experience, and that's where I feel at home the most. My experience in the work with traumatised people as well as based on the theoretical knowledge I have gained in the past 20 years as it was virtually non-existent before that. I can also testify on the basis of my work with world experts in the field of trauma and on the basis of some 2.000 hours of work under their supervision. When I became a member of the European association I had to document it all. We had local psychiatric supervision but also outside supervision. We engaged in serious analyses of the situation or situations involved in the trauma process. We do not see trauma as a disease or PTSD as a single diagnosis. We look at trauma as a process, which started at the beginning of the war and has been ongoing. Today, we have traumatised people still undergoing different processes. The symptoms are not always the same. Perhaps I could put it in a different way. According to the expert, let's take the Keilson's model about sequential traumatisation which was developed by a trauma specialist, by Dr. Baker. As part of that concept, trauma is seen as a process. The author divides, for example, refugee trauma in seven sequential parts. The first sequence is the pre-traumatic situation which is in the pre-war period, when the person was still living a normal life. Then we have the situation of expulsion, of leaving home voluntarily or under pressure, or the individual left on his or her own, or the whole family left. Then there's the period of flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As I believe I won't have more than one hour, we need to conclude this. It is all very plausible and your work is very useful, but for the needs of this trial I would like to establish what is objective and objectified as to separated from the subjective. What was objective among the things you determined? You mentioned the model where the group itself is its control group. Before the event, the same people are followed through the trauma. Did you have any research into the Srebrenica population before the events so as to be able to compare?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did you have any research into the control group so as to establish what emotional, cognitive, physical, and interpersonal disorders the traumatised people have as opposed to the people who were not traumatised?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Our organisation, and I, did not participate in that kind of research, but I did participate when the research was presented. Any research requires funds. We believed that someone -- if someone had studied or researched something, there was no need to repeat it, and that we can take it on board and fully confide it and use it for our work. We did not do research ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of course, for your work, you can use their research.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that you cannot rely on their research in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I don't think I am. I am relying on my experience and the experience of the Vive Zene expert team. I base my testimony on the findings and tests we carried out. For example, we tested thousands of people for trauma. The tests were approved and certified. If, in such tests, we established that people did have such symptoms, it is based on those tests we could determine the direction of our work. If these people are established as being re-traumatised or reliving the events or avoiding the recollection of traumatic events, then, in that way, we get some landmarks or directions as to how to approach them, and that was the basis of the Vive Zene work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe it sufficed for your work with your clients, and I do believe you have the possibility or ability of empathy. Would you characterise yourself as an empathic person?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. A person who cannot picture or feel the situation of another, then that person cannot help either. It's the basis of a therapeutic relationship, and only from that angle one can help another seeking assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we remove your work with your clients from this testimony, I need to tell you openly what it is that I'm trying to achieve. Your previous testimony in the Krstic case is full of theoretical assertions which are correct. The testimony is also full of your emotion depicting your empathy and your ability to feel the suffering of another. For the need of these proceedings, we need to separate your theoretical knowledge from your emotional and -- your emotional experience from what was objectively ascertained. Can you tell us what was it that you determined objectively, scientifically, with the use of a control group? How did you determine differentia specifica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before you answer. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm not able to follow the -- this discussion as accurately as possible, but by my count, this is approximately the third time the same question has been posed and the witness has clearly indicated the basis for the positions she's outlined previously, and I would object. One other matter is, I mean, first of all, there's a -- she is asked to deconstruct the entirety of the Krstic testimony; that is clearly impossible. But in the context of this examination, the accused has asked -- has basically posed the position that her testimony is based on theoretical propositions and she said at least twice that it was based on her experience and experience of those with whom she worked at Vive Zene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that I noted the witness started answering the question and Mr. Karadzic put his case about the nature of her testimony, I would allow the witness to proceed to answer. Could you answer as far as you can? If you remember the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to admit that I don't recall all of it because there were several topics mentioned there. One of them was empathy. The other was the theory or theoretical portion of the testimony. And the third had to do with the emotional aspect of my testimony. So I would like it to be repeated, if that's possible, the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would you say for yourself that are you a sensitive or sensual person?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Do you mean sensitive or sensible?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Would you say for yourself that you are both or one or the other?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say I'm a sensitive person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber what the difference is between empathy and projection and projective identification?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, empathy is an important component or feature -- or ability, in fact. It's the ability of the therapist, in the course of therapy, to understand what the client or the patient is undergoing. In other words, the therapist should not be judgemental but, rather, try to identify with the situation, in order to live through the patient's experience, to see what it is that is happening with that person or what has happened to the person who is now talking about his or her suffering. To make this a bit clearer, let me give you an example. For instance, if a person is two metres tall -- I need to describe it in this way although it might not be the most appropriate way. But how can a person who is two metres tall -- how does that person feel, being two metres tall? If I were to empathise with that person, I should be able to recognise how this person sees the world because I am not two metres tall. So this is the best way that I can describe this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But the projective identification, how did you shield yourself from that?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that trying to shield oneself from projecting -- from projections, projecting one's own on to the patient, is a very difficult task for each therapist if you want to be a good therapist. And in this, I needed help from my supervisors, where you repeatedly have to question your own experience and your own feelings as you're listening to what the person sitting across from you is undergoing. So is this -- am I empathising with the feelings of the person or is this something that I'm going through myself? This is a fight that a therapist has to fight for many years, and I think it is very important for a therapist to be aware of it, in order not to put him or herself into a position where they are not objective any longer. And with all my heart, or rather, with all my abilities, I constantly try to build up this mechanism that would shield me from that, and if that would not be the case, at least to be aware of what was happening to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that projective identification is something that is subconscious and how can you bring the subconscious into the conscious?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, if I am to have a role in therapy, and if that intervention is a reflection on the counter-transfer, then, of course -- then I have to bring this into my conscious, not by myself but with the assistance of my supervisor. So I have to be able to distinguish my own projections from what is objective because working with traumatised people without supervision is very difficult and it can lead to the therapist being traumatised as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to a different topic. As you know, a person cannot do this on one -- on one's own. Have you ever undergone any treatment or any therapy?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. During my training for Gestalt psychotherapy I had to undergo 100 hours of therapy of myself, and in addition to that, there were other occasions where I had to undergo therapy myself and this had to do with -- this was done in the process of my obtaining my diploma. I had occasion to be treated by -- to be -- to discuss this with all types of therapists, acting therapists, acting-out therapists, and I was -- I should be able -- I was supposed to be able to express the way in which people express their sorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's just go back to something you've said today. Would you say that in war-time conditions, losses are unpredictable, unforeseen, and are they less foreseeable than, for instance, a loss in a car accident?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, when a war starts, there is this great sense of the unknown. We know when it has begun but we don't know when it is going to end, and I think that this adds to the stressful situation. As for car accidents, they occur, and people accept the risk. In other words, people make a conscious choice. But in a war, people do not have any choice. For instance, I flew to The Hague, and I can say for myself that I never thought of a possible accident, but -- I never gave it a single thought. But this would have been my choice in any case, because I have chosen to travel. In war time, people do not have a choice. They do not take decisions on their own. They're not their decisions, or they may choose to take a decision that may turn out to be very bad for them in the long run.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I will try to be as brief as possible in my questions and you, too, please try to be as brief as possible in your answers.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the 28th Division alone in Srebrenica before the month of July 1995 had suffered some 2.000 losses?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that because that type of information did not reach Tuzla. We did not get that kind of information. I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you work with anyone who had lost someone before July 1995?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had occasion to work with people who had lost people before July 1995. If these people had -- were killed and if the rites were performed where they had the time to grieve, then the consequences would have been much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But could you -- did you observe that most of those losses were in Serb territory and that there were no funerals in Srebrenica, that these people were killed when they tried to go out to Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I can't really answer that question. I don't know anything about that. The stories that I do know about, they were stories told by my patients. Most of them women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 5814, you said that the degree of trauma or the level of trauma was very high. High in comparison to what? What was your point of reference?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, we compared that, or we had as our reference individuals who were refugees in 1992. Well, I began my work in 1994. In 1994, we had a group of women who were in-patient -- in-house patients whose husbands were in Srebrenica, not all of them, or we had cases where entire families were refugees in Tuzla, and we could use them as a reference point when comparing them to the refugees who came in 1995 who were panic-stricken, completely lost, and we saw that these people could not find their bearings. They had no idea what was going on, what was happening to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, was this based on your own experience, or do we have some objective criteria?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: We do have objective criteria as well. These criteria were developed by other organisations that we worked with. I took part in that research. I took part in the filling out of the questionnaires that were used in the research. But I also could observe their conduct because it was very easy to observe. There was a big difference between the behaviour of the people who arrived as refugees in 1995 as opposed to those before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you ever establish why it was that these people were separated before July 1995? In other words, there were men who remained in Srebrenica, whereas their family members were in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I did not understand what you meant by "separation." What did -- did we establish what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you have just said that in 1994 and before July 1995, you had cases of family members being separated, where the women and -- and children were in Tuzla, whereas the men remained in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Most of the refugees were from Zvornik and Vlasenica, while a number of men had gone to Srebrenica. And based on the stories of these women, it appears that they left their villages quite suddenly, so they got separated then. For the most part, the women had been at home, and then they were forced to be transferred to Tuzla, whereas the men stayed line, and that's how they were forced to be separated from one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, who was it that separated them?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, who took this decision on behalf of these men to remain in Srebrenica rather than leave with their families to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, what I've just mentioned had to do with 1992 and 1993. This was the beginning of the war, and from the stories of the men who survived, as well as the women, it could be inferred that they thought that Srebrenica was a safe area until it became a safe haven, which was a tiny area in a wider surrounding, and it was only then that they realised that they had taken the wrong choice because there was a lot of sense of guilt there: Why didn't we go with our families; why did we allow us to be separated from them, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So these men actually took the wrong decision. They decided to remain, whereas they sent their families to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything about that. I don't know what it was that that person -- that any particular person decided was the factor where they felt that it was threatening for them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 5815, the witness said "men and boys." How did you come up with the boys? Did you establish that there were boys there or is this something that you just took over, this language?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I did not take this over from some official documents. Rather, this was something that I picked up from my clients, from these women, because they would frequently tell you, My husband left and -- but he -- and then my -- he was a boy. He left, he was just a boy. Sometimes we would ask them how old these boys were. Sometimes they would tell us that they were 8 years old or so. We frequently had women telling us stories about their own children, and they would say then: He was just a boy. So this was not a -- the language that I picked up from some official documents or from TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were not in Srebrenica then yourself to see that for yourself. Rather, if a woman told you, My son was just a boy, you would just accept that?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, the basic principle of mine is that I would trust what the patient tells me. So if they say that it was their child, it was their boy, and if they keep repeating that this was a child, a boy who was 14 or 11, then I don't see why not believe that woman. Because that boy was no longer with her. We had cases of other children who suffered and whose behaviour was inappropriate. For instance, there were cases where a woman would celebrate a -- or throw a birthday party for a son who wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat and kindly pause between question and answer and answer and question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreters find it very difficult to catch up with your speed if you do not pause between the question and answer. Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked the witness because I saw during this previous testimony that she personally was rather successful and this method was rather successful. That was my question; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So these things are curable, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No. I cannot say that they are curable. However, people can get used to living with loss. They can accept the past. And, in the present, they can find certain contents that will give them strength to go on in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you speak about case histories, for instance, you are not writing a scientific paper that involves other things. You're just writing up a case history. Did you know about that person before the trauma?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No. No, I did not. However, when working with a woman or with a person, a patient, one can see how she had functioned before that happened. You can see on the basis of the interview what her educational background was, how she grew up, what her family relations were, and so on. On the basis of that, one can foresee what kind of a person she may have been before all that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 2827, you did not fully answer Judge Riad's question so please answer me. Is it in the same way and with same attention that you worked with Serbs -- Serb women and Croat women?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the same intentions, and with the same attention. Because pain is pain. Any person who loses a family member suffers deeply. I appreciate that pain and suffering, and I believe that it deserves the best kind of treatment that I am capable of offering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your professional findings or, rather, impressions, because we don't have before us the results of an objective research, everything that you've said, does it equally pertain to Serb, Muslim, and Croat women?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it does. Because every person that experienced extreme violence, a trauma, and a total breakdown, irrespective of ethnic or religious background or geography, such a person is in pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused by this. Are you specific, are you precise, are you careful when you speak about things? When you say, for instance, that every family is seeking 20 of its male members, is this exaggeration or what?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I did not say that each family was looking for 20 family members. I just said it was not a normal thing for a person to lose 20 male family members. I say that on the basis of the information I have. I didn't say that that was the case for each and every family. Some persons say, I have one family member missing; others say, I'm fortunate in not having any of my family members missing. But it is a fact that this kind of thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 5830, that's the page I would like to draw your attention to. Lines 7 and 8. I'm going to read it out in English because you probably do not have the transcript with you. This is part of your answer: "[In English] But there isn't a single family in Zvornik, for example, that hasn't 20 male members of its family missing ..." [Interpretation] And I did a bit of arithmetic. Then the population of Zvornik was 81.111. That is 24.000 families if three members are an average.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm not sure whether the transcript has been correctly translated because you overlapped. Did you hear what you said in Krstic? I will read it out for you, Ms. Ibrahimefendic. This is what you said: "But there isn't a single family in Zvornik, for example, that hasn't 20 male members of its family missing ..." That's the passage Mr. Karadzic is referring to. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this an exaggeration, Ms. Ibrahimefendic?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I think -- well, I think there's something missing there. Is it one person, is it 20 persons? But I cannot accept this. Maybe I was not precise enough, as you said. But this does not correspond to reality because 1.700 persons from Zvornik were missing. That the total number of missing persons from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Out of 24.000 families, 1.700 persons are missing.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you include Serbs in that figure?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: The Serb association is separate so I don't have the information. I heard that actually at a conference but I cannot tell you exactly now what the figures were.
