Because there were associations of missing persons who were ethnic Muslims, Croats and Serbs, but I cannot remember the exact number now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5834, Judge Riad went on and asked you a question about the difference. I'm going to read this out in English: "[In English] So some of the women who had to bury their dead, so they have that problem now as to the burial site of their family members ..." [Interpretation] Is this also incorrect? Is it correct that Srebrenica victims were buried in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes. But in 2000, when I said that, Potocari was not there. I mean, it hadn't been established as such. I think the year was 2003. That's when the burials in Potocari started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then on the next page, 5835, you said that during the first two days -- or, rather, on the first day of the evacuation, boys aged 10 to 12 boarded buses. And then, on the next day, children aged 12 and older were no longer allowed to board buses. What was the fate of these children who were 12 or younger? How many of them were there; and where did they end up?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: According to the information I have, these children are in mass graves. Some have been identified. A few women who were very traumatised were in our centre at that time. They had lost children who were younger. On the basis of their statements and the statements of other women that on the first day and the second day it was easier to leave Potocari than it was on the third day, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find out then how many mortal remains were found of children aged 10 to 12?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: We are a therapy and rehabilitation centre. We really do not work on that kind of research. We attend conferences, we receive information, but we do not consider this information to be part of our own work. Things that we have to communicate. I don't know. I mean, I don't deal with this. My team doesn't deal with this. The number of exhumed persons, no. We treat people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. So this is information or data provided by others; right?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5844, you mentioned that 75 persons were killed in Srebrenica at the stadium when a shell fell. Do you know who had fired that shell? Did anyone tell you anything about that?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I did not ask who had fired that shell. Rather, there were a few persons who had been at the stadium then, in 1993, who mentioned to me that several persons got killed in the stadium, and they were very angry because these victims were not being mentioned when the victims of 1995 were being mentioned. That's the only thing I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the beginning of Mr. Karadzic's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 5846, from lines 5 and 6 onwards, you say that these treatments were successful. When a woman manages to express all her emotions, the next time it's not that painful; right?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: That is right. At one point, therapy is very successful. However, if we take trauma as a process, and if we look at the problems that have to be faced within the context involved, then she relives everything that happened once again. Of course, she never reaches the stage that she was in originally but there are certain problems. For instance, if, on the 11th of July, there is going to be a burial in Potocari, then that is when women exhibit more symptoms, or, for example, when there are birthdays, anniversaries, et cetera. So there is regression then. Of course, they never go back to the point where they were when therapy had started, but there are now problems every now and then. And they are not capable of dealing with them sometimes. That means that they do need help for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5851 you say that people who receive support and therapy are very content, but the problem is that you cannot deal with everyone; right?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that is right. A lot of people need help and there are many groups that need help. People do not recognise their reactions. They think that if they do not share their pain and if they just remain silent - and this goes for all ethnic groups - in some way something is going to happen. But then they realise that nothing will happen and that they really have to seek help. They have to share their pain. They have to see that they are not alone. They have to become competent to deal with all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the next page, 5852, you say that you had some very good results among children who were treated in your centre, that a great deal of progress was achieved in terms of their behaviour.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, that's true. Because we worked with the mothers at the same time as well. If we work with children separately, we do not have results that are as good as they are when we work with the mothers too. The mothers are pre-occupied with their existential problems. They are physically present but emotionally absent, so working together yields better results as far as children are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree, Ms. Ibrahimefendic, that all the techniques that we know, starting with Freud psychoanalysis all the way to Gestalt behavioural therapy and so on, were created in peacetime and that the populations involved had not been through a war? These therapies were developed among the general population.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. But over the past ten years or so, we have come to realise how much research is being done on trauma research. And special techniques and methods have been developed in terms of working with traumatised persons. It is a fact that when the war broke out, we did not know how to work with trauma victims. We could intervene in cases of crises initially, but then what? So during the war, experts arrived from many different parts of the world, from trauma centres, from Copenhagen, for instance, and so on, and they trained us. So we learned how to deal with traumatised persons, how to establish the right kind of relationship with them, how to win their trust, and how to help these traumatised persons, in general. Working in the field of trauma is a special kind of work and does not begin or end in the therapy room, if you will. Because everything that happens around the persons involved seriously affect the patients, and how.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have more questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three or four, Your Excellency, very brief ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I will consult the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With the indulgence, we will continue for five minutes. Could you conclude in five minutes? Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you then - and I will try to phrase my question so you can just answer with a yes or no - is it true that you completed the intermediate medical school?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you worked as a nurse for how long?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I worked as a nurse for four years, but after that, I also worked with children, because I had gone to the school of pedagogy and I worked with children who were hospitalised over longer periods of time. They were treated for diabetes or tuberculosis or asthma, and I provided support to these kids because of their absence from school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the pedagogic school, that is a college-level school, correct? That's after your secondary education?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you graduated from the University of Sarajevo, the school of psychology. Did you -- were you a full time student or a part-time student?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: I was a part-time student in Sarajevo but we had classes in Tuzla. This was a department that existed in Tuzla at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are not a clinical psychologist by background?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: No. I had to undergo additional training for that, psychotherapeutic training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Are you a war veteran and since when? Is this a status that was awarded you?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, before the war, I worked at the clinical centre, and during the war, too, I worked at the medical centre. In 1994, I worked afternoons, four hours every afternoon with Vive Zene, and as of March 1st, 1996, I left the medical centre and I began working at the therapy and training centre. Now I did have a war-time work obligation, but I do not have the status of a war veteran, as you said. I just did my job at the hospital throughout those years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But did you receive the certificate, the well-known certificate that was awarded people for their work during the war?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, we all were issued these certificates because we worked for free during the war. We didn't receive any salaries or any pay, so everyone who worked at the hospital during the war, including the cleaning ladies, the porters, everyone, was issued these certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is your certificate, certificate number -- or, rather, can you tell us the number of your certificate?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, you are talking about money; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The certificate which allowed you to purchase an apartment, for instance.

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I can't remember it. This was a certificate, I can't recall what it was now, but I did use some of the money that I received then to purchase an apartment, my husband and I. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Was this a certificate that you and your husband were issued for your role during the war or your participation in the war?

utterances.speaker: TEUFIKA IBRAHIMEFENDIC
utterances.text: Well, this was a certificate that was issued -- well, I don't know. My late father was also -- he was a retired person, and he, too, was issued a certificate, so I don't know what that would mean. My mother wasn't issued any such certificate because she had never been employed but my father did, although did he not take part in the war. He did not have any role. I mean, he was there. I was in Tuzla --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies, for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Ibrahimefendic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger, do you have re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I do have one matter to inquire about unrelated to this witness's testimony before the Court leaves the bench of about 30-seconds' worth, a clarification from -- based on an order made by the Court earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Ibrahimefendic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of my colleagues, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. We'll rise all together. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think it's clear from the Court's order but I thought it best simply to confirm. When the Court indicated that it wished to have a revised list of the witnesses, the -- the 65 ter list, I understand that to mean just the list of witnesses not accompanying summaries or anything else. You just want to know what the list of witnesses -- you just want a list of witnesses to know who they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not our practice whenever there's a change we have a revised 65 ter witnesses list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm simply trying to avoid the unnecessary work that accompanies the submission of the original list. All the parties and the Court have all that information and simply provide the -- what's changed, which is the -- the -- the witnesses themselves and file something accordingly that assists the Court in that manner but doesn't entail unnecessary work on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll come back tomorrow morning. Hearing is adjourned. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
